evidence.label: Approximation Paving over Arbitrary Maximal Abelian Subalgebras
Quadratic Strong-Operator Paving over Arbitrary Maximal Abelian Subalgebras

headline: Claims to settle both paving conjectures of Popa and Vaes for every maximal abelian subalgebra of a von Neumann algebra.
scope: Self-adjoint operators in any complex von Neumann algebra, paved over any maximal abelian subalgebra, with no separability or conditional-expectation assumption.
plain: Paving means cutting an operator into a fixed number of diagonal blocks so the off-diagonal part becomes small. The Kadison–Singer problem asked this for the standard diagonal and was solved in 2015. Popa and Vaes conjectured two weaker forms of paving for every maximal commutative subalgebra. Two companion papers claim to prove both forms, with explicit counts of blocks. There is no Lean check.
doesNot: This does not give norm paving of the original operator for general subalgebras, which is known to fail. The first paper's bound is not claimed to be quadratic.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Kadison and Singer, who posed the pure-state extension problem for the diagonal subalgebra of B(ℓ²)
scorecard.significanceWhy: It would settle both parts of a 2015 conjecture of Popa and Vaes extending Kadison–Singer paving to all maximal abelian subalgebras.

explanation:
Take the 4-by-4 matrix x with 0 on the diagonal and 1 everywhere else. Its norm, the most it stretches any vector, is 3. Cut the four coordinates into two groups, {1, 2} and {3, 4}. Keep only the entries inside each group and delete the rest. This is called a pinching. What remains is two copies of the 2-by-2 matrix with 0 on the diagonal and 1 off it. Its norm is 1, a third of the original. With four groups of one coordinate each, nothing off the diagonal survives. So more groups give smaller off-diagonal parts.

Paving asks for a fixed number of groups that works for every operator. The groups come from a maximal abelian subalgebra, or MASA: a largest family of commuting operators, like the diagonal matrices. After the pinching, one subtracts an element a of the MASA. The aim is that what is left has norm at most ε times the norm of x. The original question, from Kadison and Singer, concerned the diagonal of the infinite matrix space[3]. Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava solved it by mixed characteristic polynomials[4]. For general MASAs, norm paving fails[5]. So Popa and Vaes proposed two weaker forms and conjectured both hold for every MASA[6].

The first paper claims the approximation form. Every self-adjoint operator is a strong limit of operators of norm at most three times its own. Each of these can be paved with error at most ε times its own norm[1]. The number of groups is at most C·ε^−6 for a universal constant C[2]. The second paper claims the quadratic strong-operator form[7]. Here the pinching only has to be small after a compression. The compressing projection must be close to the identity on any chosen finite set of vectors. The number of groups is at most 5 × 10⁸ · ε^−2[8]. For ε = 1/2, the bound is 2,000,000,000. Neither paper needs separability or a conditional expectation onto the MASA[9].

The obstacle is that earlier proofs split into two kinds of MASA, Cartan and singular, with different methods. Popa and Vaes noted the need to unite the two arguments[10]. The papers do this without any expectation onto the MASA. The first paper does not claim a quadratic count for its own bound[11].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The arguments are long and technical. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Major if correct: it claims both Popa–Vaes paving conjectures in full generality. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A family of operators on a Hilbert space closed under sums, products, adjoints and pointwise limits.
Maximal abelian subalgebra: a largest family of commuting operators inside the algebra, like the diagonal matrices.
